Q9000.L1t: The sources of international law are traditionally listed in Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice.
Q9000.L2t: General Assembly resolutions are generally recommendatory and are not listed among the formal sources in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute.
Q9000.L3t: A resolution's legal weight depends on its content and on how States vote and act, so it can serve as evidence of emerging or existing custom without being binding in itself.
Q9000.L4t: General Assembly resolutions are not binding in themselves but can be a material source that helps state or evidence customary rules.
Q9000.L2f: The UN Charter gives the General Assembly the power to adopt binding legislation on all member States in the same way national parliaments do.
Q9000.L3f: Because General Assembly resolutions are adopted by representatives of nearly all States, every resolution automatically codifies existing custom and so is conclusive proof of it.
Q9000.L4f: General Assembly resolutions always reflect customary law.

Q9001.L1t: Poverty is commonly measured by international institutions using a poverty line set in dollars per person per day.
Q9001.L2t: The World Bank's international poverty line was raised to $1.90 a day in 2015, and extreme poverty has fallen sharply since 1990.
Q9001.L3t: World Bank estimates put the number of people living on under $1.90 a day in 2019 at roughly 700 to 800 million out of a world population of about 7.7 billion.
Q9001.L4t: In 2019 roughly one in ten people worldwide, about 10 percent, lived in extreme poverty.
Q9001.L2f: The World Bank's international poverty line was lowered to $1.90 a day in 2015, and extreme poverty has risen since 1990.
Q9001.L3f: World Bank estimates put the number of people living on under $1.90 a day in 2019 at about 1.9 billion out of a world population of about 7.7 billion.
Q9001.L4f: In 2019 about one in four people worldwide, around 25 percent, lived in extreme poverty.

Q9002.L1t: Future interests and defeasible fees are part of the common law of estates in land.
Q9002.L2t: A grant of land to a state that includes a right of re-entry for the grantor is a conveyance subject to a condition and not an outright, unconditional gift.
Q9002.L3t: The grant says the grantor may re-enter if the land is commercially developed, using the language of a right of entry rather than words of automatic duration such as 'so long as' or 'until', so the grantor must act to end the estate.
Q9002.L4t: The state holds a fee simple subject to condition subsequent, because the grantor keeps a right of re-entry that must be exercised to end the estate.
Q9002.L2f: Under the common law, a grantor can never keep any right of re-entry after conveying a fee simple to a governmental body.
Q9002.L3f: The grant restricts commercial use and the grantor's interest arises if the land is developed, which ends the state's estate automatically without any act by the grantor, as a limitation on its duration.
Q9002.L4f: The state holds a fee simple determinable, because the estate ends automatically when the land is developed commercially.
